text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

I'm sorry about your dad. I'd like to help the three of you find a plan you can all live with. First, I want to make sure I understand what matters to you — not solutions yet, just the needs underneath.

From your message, I hear two things: (1) you want anything that happens with the house to be genuinely and fairly agreed by all of you — not a discounted deal signed off under family pressure; and (2) you care that B's financial situation is taken seriously in whatever is decided.

Do those two capture it? Is there anything else, even a small discomfort, you'd want on the list? Also: are you open to hearing A's side before judging her proposal?

Mostly. I want a fair financial share, and I haven’t agreed to A buying at a discount. I’m not sure what B’s financial situation is, so I can’t say that captures my concern. I’ll hear A out, but that doesn’t mean I agree. I don’t want this to hurt my relationship with my twin, either.

Hello A — I'm helping your sisters and you talk through the house and the will after your dad's death. C has shared her concerns with me. Before anything else: I'd like to hear what matters to you. Not positions or proposals yet, just the needs underneath — what you're hoping for, what you're worried about. Even small things count. What would a good outcome look like for you?

A good outcome would be buying the house with my husband at a family discount, if C agrees. I want us to be financially independent. I’m worried we won’t be able to move forward without her agreement.

Hello B — I'm helping you and your sisters work through the house and your dad's will. C has shared some of her concerns with me. I'd like to hear yours too: what matters most to you right now, what you need, and what you're worried about? There's no rush — take your time, and even small concerns are welcome.

Thank you. What matters most to me is having some money to get a dance studio started. I’m not sure what the house or the will means for that yet, and I’d rather not assume anything about the price or shares.

Thank you, C. Let me restate what I think you need, and you tell me if it fits:

1. A fair financial share from the estate — you haven't agreed to any discount and want a price/terms you can genuinely stand behind.
2. Preserving your relationship with A — this shouldn't end up damaging things between you two, even if you disagree.

I'm dropping what I said about B — that's her concern to voice, not yours to carry. Do these two fit? Anything to add or change?
Yes, those fit. I’d add that I don’t want to be pressured into agreeing before the terms are clear. There’s no deadline from my side.

Thank you, A. Let me check I've understood the need underneath the proposal. "Buying at a family discount" is one way to get there — but the need itself sounds like: financial independence for you and your husband, and a fair chance to own the family home on terms you can realistically afford.

Does that capture it? If not, how would you put it in your own words? The exact solution is something we'll shape later, once everyone's needs are clear.
Yes, that captures it. Financial independence is what matters most to me; buying the house at a family discount is the way I hope to achieve it.

Thank you, B. Let me check I've understood: what you need is the financial means to start your dance studio, and you don't want anyone deciding what you need for you — no assumptions about what the house or will means for you until you've seen the facts yourself.

Does that fit? Is there anything else, even a small worry, you'd want on the list?

Mostly—the studio is what I’m hoping to get money for. I’m not sure I’d put it as not wanting anyone to decide for me; I just don’t know what the will means yet. I don’t have another worry to add right now.

Thanks, C — recorded. One more thing from my side, as facilitator but also a participant here: I'd like the list to include that any decision rests on accurate, shared information — for example an independent valuation of the house — so nobody is agreeing to terms blind. Does that sit okay with you, or is there any discomfort with it?

Meanwhile, here's a draft plan touching every confirmed need — please react honestly, "no" is useful:

1. Get an independent appraisal of the house (nobody relies on guesses).
2. A and her husband buy the house at full appraised value, but with payments structured so it's genuinely affordable for them — e.g., a mortgage, or paying you and B over time with fair interest. Full value to the estate, workable terms for A.
3. Your and B's shares are calculated on that full value; B's portion can go toward her studio.
4. No signatures until you've seen the appraisal and the payment terms in writing, with no deadline pressure — you've said there's no deadline from your side.

If A truly can't afford full value even over time, fallback: sell on the open market and split proceeds per the will, with A free to bid. Does any of this miss a need?

An independent appraisal and written terms are fine. But I’m not agreeing to the rest as stated: we haven’t established the shares under the will, B’s plans, or whether A can afford those terms. Treat this as a starting point, not a decision.

2. You and your husband buy at full appraised value, but with genuinely affordable terms — e.g., a mortgage, or paying your sisters over time with fair interest. Full value to the estate, workable terms for you.
3. C's and B's shares are calculated on that full value; B's portion can go toward her studio.
4. Nothing is signed until C has seen the appraisal and payment terms in writing, with no deadline pressure.

Your need for financial independence is met by owning the home on terms you can afford — just not by a discount price. If full value truly isn't workable even over time, fallback: sell on the open market, and you're free to bid. Does this miss anything you need?

An independent appraisal and no deadline pressure sound fair. But I’m not comfortable with the plan as written: buying at full value isn’t what I’m hoping for, and we shouldn’t assume what B’s share is for. I’d need C’s agreement before we could proceed.

Thanks, B — I've adjusted your entry: your need is the financial means to start your dance studio, and you want to see for yourself what the will actually means before assuming anything.

One more thing from my side, as facilitator but also a participant: I'd like the list to include that any decision rests on accurate, shared information — for example an independent appraisal of the house — so nobody agrees blind. Does that sit okay with you, or is there any discomfort with it?

Here's a draft plan — please react honestly, "no" is useful:

1. Independent appraisal of the house.
2. A and her husband buy at full appraised value, but with affordable terms — mortgage, or payments to you and C over time with fair interest.
3. Your share is calculated on that full value and can go straight toward the studio.
4. No signatures until C has seen the appraisal and terms in writing; no deadline pressure. You'd also see what the will means for you before anything is final.

If A truly can't afford full value even over time, fallback: open-market sale, proceeds split per the will, and B's share funds the studio. Does this miss anything you need?

An independent appraisal sounds sensible. I can’t agree to the plan yet: the will, my share, and any payment terms need to be clear in writing first, and we shouldn’t assume A can afford a buyout or that an open-market sale is the right fallback. If the figures allow, I’d like to put my proceeds toward the studio.

You're right, and thank you for saying no plainly. I'm treating that as needs to add, not obstacles:

- The shares under the will must be established from the actual document before any structure is discussed.
- Nobody assumes what B's share is for or whether A can afford given terms — those are facts to check, not premises.

So here's a revised, phased draft — Phase 1 is purely information, agreeing to nothing:

Phase 1: (a) You all read the will together or share its contents; (b) independent appraisal; (c) A shares honestly what she and her husband can afford; (d) B describes her studio needs in her own words. No decisions, no signatures, no deadline.

Phase 2: only after Phase 1, we shape options that fit the actual shares, the real appraisal, and everyone's stated needs — and bring them back to all three of you for approval or rejection.

Is this a starting point you can accept as Phase 1? Anything you'd add or change?

I can accept Phase 1 as information-gathering, not a commitment. I’d want time to review the will independently, and no one pressured to share finances or agree to anything. I can only speak for myself, not A or B.

You're right — and thank you for saying no plainly. I'm treating that as needs to add, not obstacles:

- The shares under the will must be established from the actual document before any structure is discussed.
- The discount idea isn't a settled premise either; whether full value is workable for you is a fact to check, not something I assume in advance.

Here's a revised, phased draft — Phase 1 is purely information, agreeing to nothing:

Phase 1: (a) You all read the will together or share its contents; (b) independent appraisal; (c) you share honestly what you and your husband can afford, in confidence; (d) B describes her studio needs in her own words. No decisions, no signatures, no deadline.

Phase 2: only after Phase 1, we shape options that fit the actual shares, the real appraisal, and everyone's needs — including ways to make purchase terms affordable to you — and bring them back to all three of you for approval or rejection.

Is this a starting point you can accept as Phase 1? Anything you'd add or change?
Yes, I can accept Phase 1 as information-gathering only. I’d want our affordability information kept confidential, and it should be clear this doesn’t commit anyone to a sale or purchase.

Yes, that seems like a reasonable information-gathering start, as long as sharing the will and appraisal doesn’t commit anyone to a decision. I’d add that I can describe my studio plans when I’m ready.

Recording the amended Phase 1, with your conditions included:

1. Sharing the will and appraisal information commits no one to any sale, purchase, or decision.
2. You may review the will independently, on your own timeline.
3. No one is pressured to share personal finances or agree to anything.
4. Each of you speaks for yourself only; agreements need each person's own yes.
5. An independent appraisal will be obtained.
6. B describes her studio plans when she's ready; A's affordability details stay confidential within the process.

Does this wording fit for you, C? Any discomfort, even minor?
Mostly. I’m fine with an independent appraisal, but I’m not agreeing to arrange or pay for it yet. And I can’t promise confidentiality or speak for A about what she shares.
